risks.summary: Solver disagreement can invalidate strong formal claims.
Leaderboard overfitting can hide poor out-of-distribution behavior.
Artifact or manifest incompleteness can break reproducibility claims.
Assumption backlog growth can create hidden policy debt.
Slow local loops reduce feedback quality and can hide regressions.
Uncontrolled strategy-space expansion can create misleading progress signals and hide fairness/regret failures.
Raw rematch-world discovery counts can be inflated by behaviorally identical exit-policy aliases.
Hard-coding a rematch-world canonical quotient from a cooperative-starting pool can under-deduplicate richer entrant pools and distort discovery counts.
Reusing a cooperative-start rematch canonicalization cache after the entrant pool gains first-move D support can silently under-deduplicate discoveries.
Reusing a zero-noise rematch canonicalization cache under nonzero action-tremble semantics can silently under-deduplicate discoveries and distort search rankings.
Using one universal rematch canonicalization cache policy across noise topologies can either under-deduplicate discoveries or waste search budget on needless recomputation.
Keeping an unvalidated global reachability horizon for rematch canonicalization can either waste search budget or merge distinct families when the world semantics change.
Naive rematch canonicalization plans that key on full entrant signatures and a legacy global horizon can waste orders of magnitude of search budget and slow local iteration.
Vendoring the current zero-noise rematch dispatch as a bulky flat support-signature table can hide semantic structure, amplify diff noise, and make stale planner embeddings harder to audit.
An interim zero-noise planner embedding can silently drift from the regenerated regime map if the ordered-rule artifact is copied without schema and contract validation.
